title: ME03b: From Self to System - The Real Terrain of Grown-Up Leadership
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon continues his Maya narrative to argue that individual vertical development has structural limits: even a reflective, self-authored leader can be undone by an incoherent system. Maya finds Theo Dawson's Complexity Gap, which reframes her struggle as a design failure rather than personal weakness, then finds the vertical-development maps too granular to help on a chaotic Thursday. She turns instead to Becky Andree's work on high-quality connections and starts treating small relational moments as the real mechanism by which trust and capacity move. The essay's move is to recast leadership development as building system capacity between people rather than climbing a ladder of personal stages. It ends with reflection prompts on self, role and system, and is delivered as fiction-framed argument rather than data.
points: The Complexity Gap reframes leader overwhelm as a mismatch between a role's complexity and available support, not as personal weakness or burnout.
Detailed vertical-development skill maps can fail in practice because they do not tell a leader what to do in the heat of a bad morning.
High-quality connections such as a walk after a hard meeting or a simple check-in are treated as developmental infrastructure, not soft skills.
Leadership is reframed as tuning the real, informal system through presence, phrasing and timing.
The author asks leaders to aim for traction rather than transcendence, becoming the leader the system can hold.
quotes: The idea was simple and brutal: the gap is the distance between the complexity of the challenges you're facing and the developmental capacity you currently possess. It wasn’t a metaphor. It was a diagnosis. You’re not failing because you’re weak. You’re failing because the role has outgrown the scaffolding you’ve been given to hold it.

But as Maya read more, she began to feel something else: a different kind of fatigue. The skill maps were overwhelming—dozens of levels, sub-levels, diagnostic grids. It felt like a taxonomy of transcendence. And none of it told her what to do when her Thursday morning started with a budget shortfall, a team conflict, and a global VP asking for strategic clarity by 4pm. She believed in the ideas. But they weren’t landing in the heat of practice. That’s when she realised: she didn’t need more granularity. She needed something load-bearing. A framework that wouldn’t collapse under pressure.
Leadership wasn’t just an act inside a system. It was a way of tuning the system itself. Through presence. Through phrasing. Through timing.

Maya no longer believed the most developed leader was the one who could perform clarity in chaos. She believed it was the one who could hold a room long enough for something better to emerge. Who could make others feel seen, even when there was no solution. Who could let ambiguity breathe without collapsing into control or retreat.
What if leadership development isn’t personal at all? What if it's not about “being a better version of yourself,” but about building system capacity—relational, emotional, strategic.

Because maybe the real work isn’t becoming the leader the models admire. Maybe it’s becoming the leader the system can actually hold. Or better yet: the leader who helps the system hold itself together when the pressure rises.
She’s not interested in transcendence. She’s interested in traction. Not in looking down from a higher stage but in looking around and knowing what to do next.
